records.text: On June 17, 1631, Mumtaz Mahal died giving birth to her fourteenth child.
Mumtaz Mahal's grief-stricken husband, the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan, spent the next two decades building her tomb, the Taj Mahal.
On June 17, 1885, the Statue of Liberty arrived in New York Harbor from France, dismantled into 350 pieces packed in 214 crates.
The Statue of Liberty then sat boxed up for months while Joseph Pulitzer's newspaper shamed the public into paying for the pedestal it was to stand on.
On June 17, 1972, five White House operatives were arrested for burgling the offices of the Democratic National Committee.
The burglary occurred during an attempt by members of the Richard Nixon administration to illegally wiretap the political opposition.
This event became known as the Watergate scandal.
On June 17, 1939, France carried out its last public guillotining, of the murderer Eugen Weidmann at Versailles.
The crowd at the guillotining was so unruly and the smuggled film footage so scandalous that all further executions were moved behind prison walls.
On June 17, 1972, five men were caught breaking into the Democratic National Committee headquarters at the Watergate complex in Washington.
The Watergate break-in was first dismissed as a "third-rate burglary".
Two years later, the Watergate scandal forced a sitting U.S. president to resign.
Vanishing gradients in RNNs are caused by repeatedly multiplying by the weight matrix W.
Vanishing gradients make it impossible for RNNs to have long-term memory.
The basic idea of providing a shortcut for gradients, called the "constant error carousel", has been seen in ResNet.
In the mid-1990s, Schmidhuber proposed constructing RNNs from a more complex unit that has a shortcut for gradients and controls memory explicitly.
LSTM stands for long short-term memory.
In vanilla LSTM, c_t is the cell state and h_t is the hidden state.
The input gate and forget gate control whether the cell state c_t is changed to the new candidate cell state.
In LSTM, the candidate cell state c'_t is given by c'_t = tanh(W_{xc} x_t + W_{hc} h_{t-1} + b_{c'}).
The input gate i_t is given by i_t = σ(W_{xi} x_t + W_{hi} h_{t-1} + b_i).
The forget gate f_t is given by f_t = σ(W_{xf} x_t + W_{hf} h_{t-1} + b_f).
The output gate o_t is given by o_t = σ(W_{xo} x_t + W_{ho} h_{t-1} + b_o).
The cell state c_t is updated as c_t = f_t ⊙ c_{t-1} + i_t ⊙ c'_t.
The block output h_t is given by h_t = o_t ⊙ tanh(c_t).
The LSTM cell can control the cell state using the hidden state and weights.
When the forget gate is closed (f_t = 1), the cell state update becomes c_t = c_{t-1} + i_t ⊙ c'_t, resulting in ∂c_t/∂c_{t-1} = 1.
This property is known as the constant error carousel.
LSTM was developed in the mid-1990s by Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, as described in their 1995 and 1997 works.
LSTM appeared completely in its modern form in the 2000 work by Gers and Schmidhuber.
A problem with LSTM is that the gates cannot access the cell state c directly because they only see h_{t-1} = o_{t-1} ⊙ tanh(c_{t-1}).
If the output gate is closed, the behaviour of the LSTM does not depend on the cell state at all.
To address this problem, additional weight matrices called peepholes are added to the LSTM.
In peephole LSTM, the input gate is i_t = σ(W_{xi} x_t + W_{hi} h_{t-1} + W_{pi} c_{t-1} + b_i).
In peephole LSTM, the forget gate is f_t = σ(W_{xf} x_t + W_{hf} h_{t-1} + W_{pf} c_{t-1} + b_f).
In peephole LSTM, the output gate is o_t = σ(W_{xo} x_t + W_{ho} h_{t-1} + W_{po} c_{t-1} + b_o).
There exist a huge number of LSTM variations, obtained by removing any kind of gate, adding or removing each peephole, or adding or removing activation functions.
The paper "LSTM: a Search Space Odyssey" by Greff et al. (2015) provides an experimental comparison of many LSTM variations.
Some significantly simpler LSTM architectures with one less gate performed comparably to vanilla LSTM.
Gated Recurrent Units (GRU) were developed in Cho et al. (2014).
GRU also implements the constant error carousel and is simpler than LSTM.
In GRU, the update gate u_t is given by u_t = σ(W_{xu} x_t + W_{hu} h_{t-1} + b_u).
In GRU, the reset gate r_t is given by r_t = σ(W_{xr} x_t + W_{hr} h_{t-1} + b_r).
In GRU, the candidate hidden state h'_t is given by h'_t = tanh(W_{xh'} x_t + W_{hh'} (r_t ⊙ h_{t-1})).
In GRU, the new hidden state is h_t = (1 - u_t) ⊙ h'_t + u_t ⊙ h_{t-1}.
In GRU, there is no distinction between cell state and hidden state; it uses an update gate and a reset gate.
GRU has fewer matrices (6 compared to 8 or 11 with peepholes in LSTM) and fewer weights, but performs only very slightly worse than LSTM.
Because GRU has fewer parameters, you can fit more GRUs and achieve better networks within a given computational budget.
There exist other RNN variations beyond LSTM and GRU.
Józefowicz, Zaremba, and Sutskever (2015) conducted a huge experimental comparison of RNN architectures using an evolutionary approach.
They identified three interesting architectures.
The human visual system processes images through something akin to a CNN, and then attention is paid to a part while the rest is ignored.
The question of what attention means is a difficult question.
A.R. Luria studied attention, memory, and cognitive functions.
According to Knudsen (2007), attention is mostly about the interaction with working memory.
In images, humans do not see much at any given moment of time, illustrating unconscious attention.
The fovea is small.
Human eyes work in saccades, and this movement does not always help with attention.
A neural network might also need to consciously understand what to look at.
One of the first works in this area was by Larochelle and Hinton in 2010.
They modeled the positions of saccades and learned to perform a sequence of glimpses.
The development of recurrent visual attention models occurred with Mnih et al. (2014) in their work "Recurrent Models of Visual Attention".
In the model, from the previous hidden state vector h_{t-1} and a new glimpse location l_t, the function f_g produces g_t, the input for step t.
From h_{t-1} and g_t, the function f_h obtains the new hidden state h_t.
From h_t, the action a_t is given by f_a(h_t) and the next glimpse location l_{t+1} is given by f_l(h_t).
The model integrates many machine learning ideas.
Formally, the glimpse feature is g_t = f_g(x_t, l_{t-1}; θ_g).
The hidden state update is h_t = f_h(h_{t-1}, g_t; θ_h).
The glimpse location l_t is sampled from p(⋅ | f_l(h_t; θ_l)).
The action a_t is sampled from p(⋅ | f_a(h_t; θ_a)).
After an action, a new observation x_{t+1} is obtained, and a reward r_t is given at the end for correct classification.
The problem formulation is similar to reinforcement learning.
The model requires training a stochastic policy π((l_t, a_t) | s_{1:t}; θ) that outputs the next action based on the history of states.
The policy π is defined via an RNN, and the objective to optimize is J(θ) = E_{p(s_{1:T};θ)} [∑_{t=1}^T r_t].
Reinforcement learning is about optimizing such complicated functions, and methods like the REINFORCE algorithm and other policy gradient approaches can be used.
The results show the attention mechanism walking around the picture.
Ba et al. (2015) developed a deep model for recurrent visual attention.
They trained the model using variational approximations, which are also used in deep learning.
In the work by Ba et al. (2015), the model performed a task of recognizing two numbers.
The attention pattern for addition was different from that for recognition.
Gregor et al. (2015) introduced DRAW, a recurrent neural network for image generation.
DRAW is a next step in visual attention development and is a variation of the variational autoencoder.
Machine translation is an excellent test problem.
Machine translation is essentially a sequence-to-sequence problem, making it natural to use RNNs.
An RNN models a sequence X = (x_1, x_2, ..., x_T) by the chain rule: p(X) = ∏_{t=1}^T p(x_t | x_{<t}).
RNNs are used in language models to predict the next word from the previous word and hidden state.
Encoder-decoder architectures were introduced by Sutskever et al. (2014) and Cho et al. (2014).
In encoder-decoder architectures, the input is first encoded into a vector, then decoded back.
Encoder-decoder architectures can be applied to machine translation.
A problem with the encoder-decoder approach is that all information must be compressed into a single fixed-length vector.
This compression does not work well with long sequences, even for relatively long individual sentences.
A solution to the compression problem is to train special weights that indicate the importance of each part of the input for the current output.
A direct application of this idea is the use of a bidirectional LSTM with attention, as introduced by Bahdanau et al. (2014).
Soft attention methods were developed by Luong et al. (2015a; 2015b) and Jean et al. (2015).
In these soft attention models, the encoder is a bidirectional RNN, providing both forward and backward contexts.
The attention network estimates the relevance of each input word for the current translation step.
Formally, attention weights α_{tj} are computed and used to re-weigh context vectors.
The attention score is e_{tj} = a(z_{t-1}, j).
The attention weights are α_{tj} = softmax(e_{tj}; e_{t*}).
The context vector is c_t = ∑_j α_{tj} h_j.
The next state is z_t = f(s_{t-1}, y_{t-1}, c_i).
The attention weights can be visualized to show what the network is looking at.
Using attention results in a much better word order in translations.
One unusual application of attention is in the work "Grammar as a Foreign Language" by Vinyals et al. (2015).
Wu et al. (2016) described Google's Neural Machine Translation System, which aimed to bridge the gap between human and machine translation.
The basic architecture of Google Translate consisted of an encoder, a decoder, and attention.
The RNNs in Google's system were much deeper, with 8 layers in both the encoder and decoder.
Stacked LSTMs stop working well beyond 4-5 layers.
To address this, they added residual connections similar to those in ResNet.
The bottom layer of the encoder is bidirectional.
The task of generating subtitles for images is considered.
The first work on image captioning was "Show and Tell" by Vinyals et al. (2015).
The architecture of "Show and Tell" is straightforward.
The objective function is ∑_{(I,S)} log p(S | I; θ), where I is the image and S is the description.
The probability p(S_t | I, S_0, ..., S_{t-1}) is decomposed and modeled with an LSTM-based RNN.
A CNN is used to extract image features.
The "Show and Tell" model was reasonable but not very good.
Xu et al. (2015) introduced "Show, Attend, and Tell".
The paper distinguishes between soft attention and hard attention.
In soft attention, an annotation is created by computing a weighted sum: φ({a}_i, {α_i}) = ∑_{i=1}^L α_{t,i} a_i.
Hard attention is trained by maximizing a variational lower bound: L_s = ∑_s p(s|a) log p(y | s, a) ≤ log p(y | a).
The derivative of L_s with respect to parameters W is ∂L_s/∂W = ∑_s p(s|a) [ ∂ log p(y | s, a)/∂W + log p(y | s, a) ∂ log p(s|a)/∂W ].
In practice, the expectation is approximated by sampling s_t with probabilities α_i.
The 'Show, Attend, and Tell' model often performs very well.
When the 'Show, Attend, and Tell' model fails, we can attempt to understand the reasons.
In 2017, attention-based encoder-decoder architectures were found to be easier and more interesting.
The Transformer was introduced in the paper 'Attention is all you need' by Vaswani et al. (2017).
Self-attention is very effective for various sequence-to-sequence problems.
The primary motivation for the Transformer is to avoid encoding sequences with a fixed-size vector.
The Transformer is based on an encoder-decoder architecture.
Each block of the Transformer consists of a self-attention layer followed by a feedforward layer.
In the Transformer, the feedforward layer is applied independently to each input position.
In the Transformer, words are represented by vectors.
In the Transformer, the feedforward layer processes all positions in parallel.
In information retrieval, both queries and documents share the same latent space.
The methods of encoding queries and documents into this latent space may be different.
A search query is encoded into the latent space via a query encoder.
Documents are encoded into the same latent space via a different encoder.
To find the most relevant documents, we find the nearest neighbors for the query in the latent space among the documents.
One often assumes that the latent space is linear and the distance metric is the scalar product of vectors: dist(q, d) = Enc_q(q)^T Enc_d(d).
The self-attention layer receives as input a sequence of vectors x1, x2, ..., xL, which can be represented as a matrix X ∈ ℝ^{d×L}.
Queries, keys, and documents come from the input vectors x_i themselves.
The query vector q1 is obtained by multiplying x1 by a weight matrix W_Q: q1 = W_Q x1.
The query vectors q_i have dimension q, which may differ from the input dimension d (usually q < d).
The key vectors k_i are obtained by multiplying x_i by W_K: k_i = W_K x_i for i=1,...,L.
The key vectors k_i have dimension q, the same as the query vectors.
The value vectors v_i are obtained by multiplying x_i by W_V: v_i = W_V x_i for i=1,...,L.
The value vectors v_i have dimension v, and W_V ∈ ℝ^{v×d}.
In practice, v is usually equal to q.
Attention scores are computed as scalar products between queries and documents.
The scalar product q_i^T v_j is rescaled by dividing by √q.
The scores are turned into probabilities using softmax: α_{ij} = softmax( (1/√q) q_i K^T )_j.
K ∈ ℝ^{q×L} is the matrix of all keys, with K = W_K X.
The attention coefficients α_{ij} are used to form a convex combination of the value vectors v_j.
The output vector z_i is computed as z_i = softmax( (1/√q) q_i K^T ) V, where V ∈ ℝ^{q×L} is the value matrix V = W_V X.
The self-attention computation can be expressed in matrix form as Z = softmax( (1/√q) Q K^T ) V.
The defined operation constitutes a single self-attention head, not the full self-attention layer.
Multi-head attention runs H parallel self-attention heads, each with its own weight matrices W_Q^h, W_K^h, W_V^h.
After the H parallel heads, we obtain output matrices Z_1, ..., Z_H, each of size v×L.
These matrices are concatenated into Z_concat ∈ ℝ^{L×Hv}.
A weight matrix W_O ∈ ℝ^{Hv×d} is applied to compress the concatenated result: Z = (Z_concat W_O)^T.
W_O allows the self-attention layer to mix representations from different attention heads.
This mixing adds flexibility and expressiveness to the architecture.
The Transformer decoder includes masked self-attention and encoder-decoder attention layers.
Masked self-attention prevents the decoder from attending to future tokens, as it generates tokens autoregressively.
Masking is achieved by inputting the full sequence and masking future positions within the self-attention layers.
Formally, masking sets the softmax arguments for future tokens to −∞, resulting in zero attention weights.
Encoder-decoder attention is a variant of self-attention that conditions on the encoder's output.
In encoder-decoder attention, the queries come from the previous decoder layer, representing already generated output tokens.
In encoder-decoder attention, the key and value vectors come from the decoder.
Informally, encoder-decoder attention performs retrieval on the encoder's output using queries from already generated tokens.
Formally, in encoder-decoder attention, there are L terms in the softmax argument per vector, and the number of outputs equals the number of inputs.
Byte-pair encoding is based on Huffman coding.
An example vocabulary for byte-pair encoding is: {cat:10, pet:12, mat:5, rat:8, eats:4}.
In byte-pair encoding, the vocabulary is split into individual symbols, and pairs of symbols are counted.
From the example, the symbol counts are: c:10, a:27, t:39, p:12, e:16, m:5, r:8, s:4.
The pair counts are: ca:10, at:27, pe:12, et:12, ma:5, ra:8, ea:4, ts:4.
The most frequent pair 'at' is replaced with a new symbol Z, updating the vocabulary.
After replacement, the word forms become: {cZ:10, pet:12, mZ:5, rZ:8, eZs:4}.
The updated symbol counts are: c:10, Z:27, t:12, p:12, e:16, m:5, r:8, s:4.
The updated pair counts are: cZ:10, pe:12, et:12, mZ:5, rZ:8, eZ:4, Zs:4.
The next most frequent pair (pe or et, count 12) is replaced with symbol Y.
After replacing with Y, the word forms are: {cZ:10, Yt:12, mZ:5, rZ:8, eZs:4}.
This process is repeated until the desired vocabulary size is achieved.
In the Transformer, each token can directly attend to any other token, ignoring the distance between them.
This is advantageous compared to RNNs.
The Transformer has a fixed bounded context window.
Since attention weights are uniform across positions, the self-attention layer loses sequence order information (e.g., which tokens are adjacent).
Positional encodings are added to provide the Transformer with artificial sequence information.
Positional encodings are vectors added to token embeddings to indicate the token's position.
Using an increasing integer sequence (1,2,3,...) for positional encoding fails to generalize to longer sequences and causes ill-defined behavior for large values.
Using a fixed interval like [0,1] divided into pieces does not convey the actual number of tokens between positions (e.g., the distance 0 to 0.5 could represent 1 or 100 tokens).
Positional encodings are computed using sine and cosine functions of different frequencies: PE(pos,2i) = sin(pos/10000^{2i/d}) and PE(pos,2i+1) = cos(pos/10000^{2i/d}).
In these formulas, pos is the token position and d is the embedding dimension.
Self-attention is computationally important.
Self-attention reduces path lengths between words.
Self-attention potentially adds interpretability.

The intermediate per-head output matrices are larger than the final output.
The input matrix X has dimensions L×D, where L is the number of tokens and D is the feature dimension.
X is processed by H attention heads, producing matrices Z₁ through Z_H.
Each head output Z_i is a matrix of size L×d, where d is the per-head dimension.
Concatenating all Z_i matrices yields a matrix of size L×(H·d).
H·d is larger than D.
The concatenated matrix is passed through a feedforward layer (multiplication by a weight matrix) to produce the final Z.
This feedforward layer produces a final Z matrix of size L×D.
Multi-head attention provides variety because different heads produce different projections of the input vectors.
This variety increases the model's expressive power.
If the per-head dimension d were equal to the model dimension D, multi-head attention would be infeasible to train due to its size.
The encoder consists of self-attention, layer normalization, and a feed-forward network.
The decoder involves additional components beyond the encoder.
During inference, when predicting the next token, masked self-attention operates as regular self-attention on the current prefix.
Training a transformer on a sequence of length N can be viewed as N separate training samples, each predicting the next token from a prefix.
Running the decoder separately for each prefix is inefficient.
In practice, the entire sequence is processed at once, using masks to prevent attending to future tokens.
Masked self-attention enforces causality: each position can only attend to previous positions.
Masks are implemented by setting attention weights to zero for positions that should not be attended to.
In encoder-decoder attention, the query matrix Q is derived from the decoder input X by multiplying with W^Q.
In encoder-decoder attention, the key matrix K and value matrix V are derived from the encoder outputs by multiplying with W^K and W^V respectively.
In encoder-decoder attention, the queries and the keys/values come from different sources, unlike self-attention where all come from the same X.
In encoder-decoder attention, the attention matrix is not necessarily square because the number of queries can differ from the number of keys.
The number of keys must equal the number of values, but the number of queries can be different.
Having queries from one source and keys/values from another is a standard design in transformers, dating back to the original transformer decoder.
A value vector is a projection.
The projection is trained for the input vectors.
Input vectors are abstract representations of tokens.
After training, attention heads often perform understandable, interpretable, and intuitive operations.
There is an example of a one-layer self-attention head designed to output the matching key for the input.
In this example, the attention matrix shows that the attention head attends to the correct position.
Another example illustrates that the attention weight matrix does not have to select a single token.
Attention matrices often resemble permutation matrices.
When attention matrices resemble permutation matrices, they encode pairwise relationships between tokens, matching each input to another input.
Attention matrices do not have to be permutation matrices.
Attention matrices can have more complicated patterns, such as an orientation matrix where queries attend to all tokens.
In one example, tokens are split into groups of sizes 3, 3, 3, 1, and 3, and tokens within each group attend uniformly to each other.
Widely distributed attention is possible, where a token attends to all tokens.
Tokenization is not the main subject of the lecture because the focus is on computer vision.
Tokenization connects to coding theory and Huffman coding.
Intuitively, a token might be thought of as a word in text.
Tokens cannot simply be words because there are too many words.
Lemmatization would lose grammatical information.
Different grammatical forms must be treated as separate words.
There are typos in real text.
Dropping out-of-vocabulary words would cause loss of information.
Including all typo variants would make the dictionary enormous, with millions of words.
A smaller vocabulary is needed.
Characters can be used as tokens.
Text can be viewed as a sequence of characters.
Character sequences are a natural partition for most languages.
Character-level tokenization is too fine-grained.
There are at most a couple hundred characters, including punctuation and capitals.
With characters, one can have an embedding matrix of several hundred vectors.
Character-level tokenization leads to very long sequences.
The practical limit on context size is about one million tokens.
One million tokens represent many more words if they are word tokens rather than character tokens.
It is desirable to have tokenization closer to word-level than character-level.
The problem is how to choose intermediate tokenization between characters and words.
The algorithm is byte-pair encoding (BPE).
BPE is commonly used in machine learning.
BPE has nothing to do with machine learning.
BPE is essentially Huffman coding from information theory.
In BPE, starting from characters, the most frequent pair of characters is merged into a new token.
In an example, the pair "@" is chosen as a new token Z.
All occurrences of the pair are replaced with the new token.
Original characters cannot be deleted from the vocabulary because they may appear separately.
The replacement reduces word length.
The process adds a token in an optimal way.
The merging process is repeated.
After replacement, counts and pairs are updated only for affected tokens.
The next most frequent pair is chosen and replaced.
BPE is simple and straightforward.
BPE can be stopped at any desired vocabulary size.
By running BPE until the vocabulary reaches 100,000 tokens, one obtains a size between character-level and full word-level.
BPE first captures common suffixes like "-ed" and "-tion".
In the resulting tokenization, common words become single tokens and uncommon words become multiple tokens.
Transformers can connect any token to any token in one step, which is their biggest strength.
Transformers lose word order.
Recurrent networks naturally incorporate word order because adjacent tokens are processed in sequence.
The attention weight matrix does not inherently encode adjacency or distance.
Transformers are invariant to token order, which is problematic.
It is desirable to preserve word order.
In practice, positional encodings are added to token embeddings to encode token position.
A naive approach is to use one-hot encoding of position indices.
A desired property of positional encodings is that the difference vector between positions i and j is similar to the difference vector between positions i+k and j+k for any k.
For any pair of positions the same distance apart, the difference in their positional encodings should be consistent.
The original Transformer used a positional encoding based on a counting system analogous to binary numbers.
In binary numbers, digits oscillate with increasing periods.
The original Transformer used sinusoidal functions with different frequencies to encode positions.
The original approach to positional encodings was a positional system for counting.
The current approach to positional encodings is called RoPE (rotary positional encodings).
Rotary positional encodings involve rotation, which is a kind of circular motion.
In RoPE, you take the vector x and consider its components in pairs (two by two).
In RoPE, you break x into pieces of two numbers, which are like two-dimensional vectors.
In RoPE, the pairs are denoted as (x1, x2), (x11, x12), (x21, x22), and so on.
In RoPE, each two-dimensional part can be rotated by various angles.
Rotating a single number is not meaningful.
A vector of two numbers can be rotated because it is a vector on a plane.
Rotary encodings take a two-dimensional vector and multiply it by rotation matrices.
The positions are encoded as coefficients to these rotations.
The rotation matrix used in RoPE is [[cos(kθ), sin(kθ)], [-sin(kθ), cos(kθ)]].
There is a basic angle θ in RoPE.
In RoPE, vectors are rotated by multiples of θ.
Rotating a vector by kθ and then by Lθ is equivalent to rotating it by (k+L)θ.
Rotary positional encodings provide nice arithmetic properties and seem to have better properties.
In sinusoidal positional encoding, the dot product between two positional encoding vectors depends only on the offset (i - j).
That the dot product depends only on the distance is a desired property.
Rotary positional encodings also yield a matrix with a diagonal structure.
Along each diagonal, the distance between positions is the same, leading to the same dot product between positional encodings.
Scaling by the square root of d is necessary to prevent getting closer and closer to one-hot representations.
Without scaling, entropy is lost after the softmax.
